Introduction

For Quantum SDK 2.0 we decided to review everything: from the entity model and code generation to photon transport layers and Unity tooling.

The basic principles remain the same (seamless predict/rollback gameplay engine), but there are very important changes. Although many of them are internally they still drive how exposed APIs comes to be.

This document is a quick reference to the important changes and includes thorough explanations and code snippets to guide you through the new basic aspects of Quantum.

Back To Top

Hello Quantum 2.0

If this is your first time using Quantum, please start by watching this introductory video going over the basics.

Back To Top

Highlights

  • Memory Model: Quantum now implements a sparse-set ECS model (similar to enTT). This means entities are just references to collections of components. The most important advantages of this are memory consumption is proportional to the amount of instantiated entities and components can be added and removed dynamically.
  • Dynamic Collections: In addition to fixed sized "arrays", Quantum now adds full predict/rollback support to dynamic collections inside the game state.
  • Dynamic Asset DB: Assets are now loaded dynamically when required (first time used) or when explicitly requested (background thread loading). Everything is thread safe from parallelized systems, and it is now also possible to add assets dynamically to the DB even on predicted frames.
  • Entity Prototypes: New asset type (+ Unity editors) for entity compositions and data, so you can easily instantiate pre-defined entities (including prefabs placed in a game scene which are baked into the Map and automatically instantiated).
  • Physics Engines: A new split-components model (PhysicsCollider, PhysicsBody + per-entity toggleable physics callbacks and joints, both in 2D and 3D versions) mean a lot more expressive power and control of physics. This is reflected in completely revised APIs and a brand new 2D physics engine with a much improved performance.
  • Online Menu Scene + Photon Realtime: Completely reviewed reference Menu scene, with a lot of quality of life improvements and extra features out of the box + new iCommunicator implementation based on the bare photon realtime API (removed PUN, although still possible to import PUN2 if necessary).
  • Task Profiler: High performance CPU task/thread profiling with very low overhead, including support for remote profiling even IL2CPP builds. Automatically profiles custom systems.

Back To Top

Entities And Components

In the sparse-set ECS memory model, entities are just indices (EntityRef is a custom type of index type with some additional information such as versioning) to a collection of components (kept in dynamically allocated sparse sets).

To create a new entity instance, just use this (method returns an EntityRef):

var e = frame.Create();

Entities do not have pre-defined components, to add a Transform3D and a PhysicsCollider3D to this entity, just type:

var t = Transform3D.Create();
frame.Set(e, t);

var c = PhysicsCollider3D.Create(Shape3D.CreateSphere(1));
frame.Set(e, b);

These two methods are also useful:

// destroys the entity, including any component that was added to it.
frame.Destroy(e);

// checks if an EntityRef is still valid (good for when you store it as a reference inside other components):
if (frame.Exists(e)) {
  // safe to do stuff, Get/Set components, etc
}

To iterate over entities, use one of these four options:

a) Component iterators:

foreach(var transform in frame.GetComponentIterator<Transform3D>()) {
  // The transform returned in this instance is a copy of the transform component
  transform.Position += FPVector3.Forward * frame.DeltaTime;

  // EntityRef
  var e = transform.Entity;

  // Remember to Set the new values on the component attached to the entity.
  frame.Set(e, transform);
}

b) or the new generic component filters (up to 8 has/not/any components):

var es = frame.Filter<Transform3D, PhysicsBody3D>();
// Next fills in copies of each of the components + the EntityRef
while (es.Next(out var e, out var t, out var b)) {
  t.Position += FPVector3.Forward * frame.DeltaTime;
  // remember to set the new transform data back to the entity
  frame.Set(e, t);
}

You have options for any and without semantics using the ComponentSet struct:

var notInterested = ComponentSet.Create<PhysicsBody3D>();
var theseAreFine = ComponentSet.Create<CharacterController3D, NavMeshAgent>();
var filtered = f.Filter<Transform3D, Prefab>(without: notInterested, any: theseAreFine);

c) or component block iterators to get fastest possible direct access via pointers (handle with extreme care):

foreach(var t in frame.Unsafe.GetComponentBlockIterator<Transform3D>()) {
    t->Position += FPVector3.Forward * frame.DeltaTime;
}

d) of course, component filters also allow you to grab unsafe pointers:

var es = frame.Filter<Transform3D, PhysicsCollider3D>();
// NextUnsafe fills in pointers for each of the components + the EntityRef
while (es.NextUnsafe(out var e, out var t, out var b)) {
  // this is a pointer, no need to call frame.Set()
  t->Position += FPVector3.Forward * frame.DeltaTime;
}

Also possible to check dynamically if an entity contains a certain component type, and get a pointer to the component data directly from frame:

if (frame.Has<Transform3D>(e)) {
  var tP = frame.Unsafe.GetPointer<Transform3D>(e);
}

With ComponentSet, you can do a single check if an entity has multiple components:

var components = ComponentSet.Create<CharacterController3D, PhysicsCollider3D>();
if (frame.Has(e, components)) {
  // do something
}

Removing components dynamically is as easy as:

frame.Remove<Transform3D>(e);

Back To Top

Dynamic Collection

In addition to entities and components being dynamically instantiated, Quantum's new custom allocator allowed us to expose blittable collections as part of the rollback-able game state. Please visit the ECS->DSL page in the Manual section for more information about the dynamic collections available in Quantu and how to use them.

Here is how you can store a reference to a generic List in a component or struct definition (inside a Quantum .qtn DSL file). Notice you can use any of the other blittable types of the game-state as the generic type:

component Targets {
  list<EntityRef> Enemies;
}

Dynamic collections are stored as references inside components and structs, so you need to manually allocate them when initializing, and more importantly, freeing them when not needed anymore.

Important to remark a couple of things:

  • List contents are fully rollback-able (kept inside Quantum's frame custom memory allocator);
  • Various components can refence the same List instance;

Here are the basic API methods for dealing with these Lists:

// instantiating the component (later set it to an entity, as explained in the previous section)
var targets = new Targets();
// allocating a new List (returns the blittable reference type - QListPtr):
targets.Enemies = frame.AllocateList<EntityRef>();

To actually get the list struct to add/remove/iterate, resolve it from frame:

var l = frame.ResolveList(targets.Enemies);
// all expected API emthods of a list (Add/Remove/Contains/IndexOf/RemoveAt/[], etc (can also be iterated over, etc):
l.Add(anEntityRef);
//

If a list is not needed anymore, it is mandatory to de-allocate it from the frame data, leading to a memory leak otherwise (we are working to detect these in debug mode):

// receives the list QListPtr reference
frame.FreeList(targets.Enemies);

Back To Top

Dynamic Asset DB

Quantum's AssetObject database has been re-written from scratch and now adds the following important features:

  • thread-safe dynamic loading of assets from storage (both asynchronous and deterministic synchronous).
  • predict/rollback support for adding assets during simulation (you can now add assets even on predicted frames).
  • Better tooling: Asset DB inspector (loaded state, full list of assets, etc.), Unity asset-bundles based loader, etc.

The first noticeable change is the addition of an asset DB inspector, from which you can test loading/disposing assets (you can even do this while the game is running, to test the automatic re-loading of assets in use):

Most of the changes are hidden internally, and the base AssetObject class remains the same, so you can expect the same DSL and polymorphism support as before.

When a type-safe AssetObject instance is required, it needs to be resolved via the Frame object like this:

// based on an AssetRef (which stores the new custom guid):
var asset = frame.FindAsset<CustomAssetClass>(assetRef.Id);

// or based on its resource path (optional, not really required):
asset = frame.FindAsset<CustomAssetClass>("folder/myAssetPath");

The calls above are very fast when the asset is already loaded, but are thread-safe blocking calls in case the asset is not yet loaded, so they are guaranteed to be deterministic, no matter the current loaded state of the asset in different machines.

If you know in advance what assets will be needed (think about a bit Map or set of Navmeshes), you can schedule background-thread asynchronous asset loading (safe to call from the Unity-side, either before starting a match or at runtime):

// that is it:
frame.LoadAsset(assetRef.Id);

The new AssetRef struct is based on 64bit guids. Your custom asset classes should keep references to other assets by storing AssetRefs (the code-generated type-safe Unity drawers are displayed accordingly of course):

partial class MyAssetType {
  // this will support type-safe drag & drop on Unity editor:
  public AssetRefMyOtherType Other;
}

Adding asset object instances during runtime now supports predict/rollback (so can be done in non-verified frames just fine):

var a = new MyCustomAsset();
// fill in data (Quantum generates the AssetGuid)
var assetGuid = frame.AddAsset(a);

Another example of these implications are EntityRoot-based prefabs, these are now explicitly baked as DB assets thus generating a Prefab AssetRef which can be stored with drag & drop support (for instance as part of a CharacterSpec asset class):

partial class CharacterSpec {
    public AssetRefView ViewAsset;
}

Then, when instantiating an entity for a character, just pass the AssetRef to the Prefab component:

var viewAsset = f.FindAsset<EntityView>(spec.ViewAsset);
var view = View.Create(viewAsset);
frame.Set(e, view); // adding a view component to entity

There is also a much better data-driven approach to pre-define entities now (next section).

N.B.: The absence of AssetLinks means it is not possible to just create a .Unitypackage file to migrate a DB from a Quantum 1.2.x project. For this reason, we are working on a 1.2 -> 2.0 DB exporter/importer to perform this operation.

Back To Top

Entity Prototypes

You can define entity compositions -i.e. which components are included in them- and data -values of the component fields- directly from the Unity editor.

As most data-driven features in Quantum, these are stored as asset objects (so all new features like dynamic loading, etc., are included), and the tooling includes convenient custom drawers.

From Unity, the prototype system is driven by the EntityPrototype script and auto-generated EntityComponent MonoBehaviours.

To create a new prototype asset, use the context menu (create/quantum/entity prototype) or add just the EntityPrototype script to any Prefab and start appending the component prototype scripts from the drop down list in it:

Once the prototype is baked as a DB asset, this is all the code you need to create a new entity based on the prototype:

var prototypeAsset = frame.FindAsset<EntityPrototype>(assetRef.Id);
var e = frame.Create(prototypeAsset);
// that is it...

Even more conveniently, it is also possible to create "scene" entity-prototypes directly as game objects inside Unity Scenes, which are baked into the Map object and automatically instantiated when the map is loaded to the Quantum simulation. You can achieve that by placing the previously created prefab on the scene or just by adding the EntityPrototype script to any Game Object that is already there.

Here are three entities directly added to the scene (no code required) from the prototype shown in the previous image (immediately moving towards the pre-set target position - from the navmesh agent prototype component):

Back To Top

EntityView

You can also add the EntityView MonoBehaviour to the any prefab/scene game object that is an entity prototype. If done this way, the prefab/scene game object will have both the prototype and the view embeded into a single serialized unit.

You can also point to a separate, non embedded EntityViewAsset to assign the view to be instantiated for a prototype.

Back To Top

Physics Engines

Aside from the internal changes, such as the much lighter and faster new 2D physics core, a lot of improvements have been made to the physics APIs.

Collider And Body Components

Every exposed type and method signature has been revised for consistency, but most importantly, the old components DynamicBody/DynamicBody3D are replaced by these (which can be used in combination):

  • PhysicsCollider2D/PhysicsCollider3D
  • PhysicsBody2D/PhysicsBody3D

For more information please read the manual entries in Physics->Collider and Body Components.

Splitting the old DynamicBody components into these lets the developers express better the desired physics behavior, and also helps keep memory consumption controlled. Follows a few code snippets for how to use the recommended pattern for instantiating and adding these components to an entity (of course, the entity prototyping system can be use to initialize these from Unity/DB).

To create an entity with a transform and collider, so it becomes an obstacle that can be repositioned anytime (there are several overloads for each Create() method whose meanings are straightforward):

var entity = f.Create();
// this sets rotation as FPQuaternion.Identity, yay!
var transform3D = Transform3D.Create();
var collider = PhysicsCollider3D.Create(Shape3D.CreateSphere(1));
f.Set(entity, transform3D);
f.Set(entity, collider);

The code above is enough to make the entity an obstacle or trigger (if collider is set for that). All the following components are optional.

To make this entity actually be driven by physics (so also to let you add force, torque, modify velocity, etc. - collider is used to compute inertia):

var body3D = PhysicsBody3D.CreateDynamic(mass: FP._1);
f.Set(entity, body3D);

Additionally to the publicly exposed components (collider and body), there are two internally kept ones (which can be seen on the state inspector when being used): PhysicsCallbacks and PhysicsJoints.

We decided to control these internally, and just expose APIs to set/reset the internal flags and data.

Back To Top

Callbacks

Collisions are called on a per-entity basis, and by default colliders do not receive any callback.

To actually receive collision/trigger callbacks for an entity, add the appropriate component with the desired callback flags set (this means full rollback-able control per entity):

// this will set this entity to receive callbacks for dynamic collisions (but no triggers, and no statics).
// callbacks ar still signals, but now you can assume the entity order to mean the first one has the callback flags set.
// Two entities can receive the callback for a single collision event, assuming bith have the flags set).
var flags = CallbackFlags.Dynamic | CallbackFlags.Collision;
frame.Physics3D.SetCallbacks(frame, entity, flags);

There is an internal component to hold dynamic joint constraints to bodies (anchor entity only requires a transform). Other joint types, besides spring/damper will be added with new SDK releases:

// Params: spring, damper, distance, anchor entity
var joint = Joint3D.CreateSpringDamper(10, 2, 2, otherEntity);
var jointIndex = frame.Physics3D.AddJoint(entity, joint);

Also included are methods for Remove/RemoveAt.

Back To Top

Transport Layer + Online Menu Scene

We removed the custom PUN package from Quantum and replaced it with the stock Photon Realtime SDK

  • Version: Photon Realtime 4.1.2.20 (12. December 2019 - rev5266)
  • Download the Latest Photon Realtime Unity SDK here

Back To Top

Why

  • Quantum was only using the Realtime features on the PUN library
  • Quantum was based on an older version of PUN
  • The old version was not playing well together with other Photon SDKs like Chat or Voice for example

Back To Top

How

The class PhotonNetwork.LoadBalancingPeer (PUN) is being replaced by Photon.Realtime.LoadBalancingClient (Realtime) and subsequentially SendOperation() with OpRaiseEvent() as seen in ´QuantumNetworkCommunicator.cs`.

PhotonNetwork.ServerSettings got a custom replacement in PhotonServerSettings which is just wrapping Photon.Realtime.AppSettings into a ScriptableObject.

The new class QuantumLoadBalancingClient.cs derives from Photon.Realtime.LoadBalancingClient and performs caching the BestRegionSummary in PlayerPrefs. It can be used to start a Photon connection or use its base class. The latter being the one that needs to be handed to the QuantumNetworkCommunicator to start the Quantum game in the end.

Photon.Realtime does connection and room handling basically the same way as PUN did. Caveats when moving to Realtime are: * AutoJoinLobby must be done by hand:

public void OnConnectedToMaster(){
  LoadBalancingClient.OpJoinLobby(null);
}
  • The Room list is not cached locally anymore and is send in chunks. See UILobby.UpdateRoomList() for a demonstration.

Photon SDKs are now located in the Asset/Photon folder: Alongside the preinstalled Realtime developers can add Voice and Chat for example.

Back To Top

Demo Menu

The demo menu showcases with simple UI how to get into a Quantum game with other players using Photon.Realtime and should be the starting point of getting players together into your game scene when starting the development.

It is based on the former UILobby from Quantum 1.x and focuses on getting players faster into games with less clicks and without limiting the configuration potential. We refrain from using the Lobby and instead use OpJoinRandomOrCreateRoom (see Quantum.Demo.UIConnecting) which greatly reduces the overhead of room creation and it anyway a more appropriate use case for the majority of online games.

A new feature is PhotonPrivateAppVersion selectable on the first UI screen that limits the random matchmaking to clients that were build from the same machine. For this purpose a unique GUID is generated and stored locally that differs to everyone else. To mitigate that older build can still connect, regenerate that GUID when creating a new build in your custom build pipeline. This also greatly improves the testing for one developer that was plagued by other devs connecting to his rooms and causing desyncs. Setup PhotonAppVersions to separate testing groups even further.

Instead of changing the source code a RuntimeConfig can now be injected in a data-driven way into the menu. Load the menu.scene and look for a RuntimeConfigContainer.

Additionally a proposal to manage new (we expand Quantum regions regularly) PhotonRegions is shown.
